items.titel: Scandal-hit EU innovation agency disputes auditors’ finding that €8.7m may be unrecoverable
items.anriss: The European Institute of Innovation & Technology (EIT), which received €435m in taxpayer money in 2025, is the only EU agency out of a total of 43 whose accounts did not yield a “clean opinion” in the most-recent audit.

absaetze.t: The European Institute of Innovation & Technology (EIT), which received €435m in taxpayer money in 2025, is the only EU agency out of a total of 43 whose accounts did not yield a “clean opinion” in the most-recent audit.
The accounts of the innovation hub did not properly reflect an €8.7m recovery uncertainty, according to a report by European Court of Auditors (ECA) last week.
Several dozen of its auditors check the EU agencies every year to form a basis for Brussels bodies to later make decisions on funding.
The financial audit delivers the latest blow to the EIT, an EU agency whose bodies have faced several investigations over spending.

“Taxpayers should be concerned,” said Kenneth Haar, researcher at Corporate Europe Observatory, a watchdog. “I find it amazing and worrying to see the EIT house is still not in order, though it was more than two years ago that investigators first stepped in.”

Lead ECA auditor Petri Sarvamaa said, “The good news is that public money is managed well overall. But the weaknesses we identified also show why strong checks are essential in protecting EU taxpayers’ money.”
Based in Budapest, the EIT aims to boost European competitiveness by connecting enterprises, researchers and education.

It distributes funds to sector-specific partnerships called knowledge and innovation communities (KICs). And the spending habits of some of these KICs have caused a financial and reputational headache for EIT bosses.
The ECA’s report of the EIT’s financial accounts published on Thursday (29 October) said the innovation hub’s grant payments were affected by “a material level of error”.
But because verification checks were incomplete, it “could not provide an estimated error rate” of grant payments.
The report also flagged that the agency could fail to recover €8.7m. At least some of this is due to EIT Manufacturing, a KIC which filed for liquidation in March 2026.

The audit states: “An impairment should have been recognised [...] EIT receivables and net assets are overstated by €8.7m, impairment expenses are understated by the same amount, and the economic result for the year is overstated by €8.7m.”
But the innovation and tech agency disagreed with these findings.

While the EIT acknowledged that an impairment should have been recognised, it told auditors the amount is actually up to €0.5m, not €8.7m. The chance of recovering the money, the EIT said, is “very likely”.
Specifically, it expects to recover €5.9m via the so-called Mutual Insurance Mechanism (MIM), and €2.3m by offsetting money owed by EIT Manufacturing.
The court of auditors also said risks are “amplified” by the use of multiannual grants reported and cleared only every 18 months. In response, the EIT said it is moving to 12-month reporting periods.
“I think this is all about the pitfalls of letting private actors handle public money, and with relatively few strings attached.... it invites the sort of trouble we have seen,” added Haar.
“At another level, I believe it is a symptom of the laissez-faire approach of the EU institutions to start-ups and innovation.”
Pumped up KICs?
EU law sets out that in their seventh year, KICs should be subject to scrutiny before they can receive another seven years of taxpayer money.
They are envisioned to become financially independent and sustainable after 15 years of existence.
In 2025, the digital, clean energy, and climate change KICs were due to be independent as they reached their 15th birthdays.
But in 2026-27 two of them reportedly received a shared total of €43m from the EIT, which pumped up KICs with EU funds past the supposed expiration date.

items.titel: Trump approval rating near record low on eve of US midterm elections: Poll
items.anriss: Only 32 percent of voters approve of Trump's job performance in the latest Reuters/Ipsos poll.

absaetze.t: Only 32 percent of voters approve of Trump’s job performance in the latest Reuters/Ipsos poll.
Ahead of the United States midterm elections, President Donald Trump’s job approval rating continues to sit near a record low, according to a Reuters/Ipsos poll.
Some 32 percent of respondents approved of Trump’s handling of the presidency, 1 percentage point above his rating two weeks ago.

Meanwhile, the Republican Party continues to be unpopular among those polled: When asked whether they would vote for a generic Democrat or Republican candidate, 46 percent of respondents preferred Democrats compared with 38 percent preferring Republicans.

Trump himself is not on the ballot, but he has repeatedly told his supporters to vote as if they are voting for him. If the Republican Party loses control of the US Congress, Trump has warned, Democrats may seek to impeach him for a third time.

Trump’s approval rating has dropped steadily, polls suggest, especially since the launch of the US-Israel war on Iran on February 28. The conflict has driven up petrol and diesel prices and has had secondary effects for US consumers worried about inflation and the economy.

The president embarked on a nearly monthlong campaign blitz ahead of the November 3 midterms in an effort to shore up support for Republican candidates, who are trying to retain control of the US House of Representatives and Senate.

Trump wrapped up his campaigning on Monday afternoon with a rally in Washington, DC, at the Lincoln Memorial Reflecting Pool. The president has devoted significant attention to the site as part of his attempt to renovate the capital. The job ran months late and cost more than 10 times its original estimate, with a special liner for the pool that Trump touted peeling away soon after it was installed.

“It was a work of art that never worked, but now it will work,” Trump said at the rally. He spent much of his speech on his renovation plans for the city, including a “Triumphal Arch”, which is facing legal challenges.
Trump seemed to acknowledge on Monday that his campaigning might not deliver the results he wants for his party, but said this was the political norm for midterm elections.
“For some reason, the sitting president doesn’t win the midterms,” Trump said. “But we gave this a very strong shot.”

items.titel: Piratage de Binance: la Corée du Nord qualifie les accusations du FBI de «grave provocation politique»
items.anriss: La Corée du Nord a dénoncé mardi les accusations du FBI selon lesquelles Pyongyang serait à l'origine du piratage record de 6,3 milliards de dollars contre la plateforme d'échanges de cryptomonnaies Binance, la sœur du dirigeant Kim …

absaetze.t: La Corée du Nord a dénoncé mardi les accusations du FBI selon lesquelles Pyongyang serait à l'origine du piratage record de 6,3 milliards de dollars contre la plateforme d'échanges de cryptomonnaies Binance, la sœur du dirigeant Kim Jong-un les qualifiant de « grave provocation politique ».
3 min Temps de lecture

Kim Yo-jong a déclaré dans un communiqué diffusé par l'agence de presse d'État KCNA que les affirmations du FBI relevaient d'une « rhétorique absurde n'apportant rien de nouveau », compte tenu des précédentes accusations américaines selon lesquelles la Corée du Nord aurait déjà été responsable du piratage de ByBit en février 2025.

« C'est une grave provocation politique à l'égard de la RPDC que les États-Unis trompent l'opinion publique internationale, comme si tous les cybercrimes commis dans différentes parties du monde étaient de notre fait », a déclaré Mme Kim, utilisant l'acronyme désignant la République populaire démocratique de Corée, nom officiel de la Corée du Nord.
Le FBI accuse la Corée du Nord

La police fédérale américaine (FBI) a accusé samedi 31 octobre la Corée du Nord d'être l'auteur du vol de 6,3 milliards de dollars de cryptomonnaies grâce au piratage de la plateforme Binance. « La République populaire démocratique de Corée (Corée du Nord) est responsable du vol de plus de 6 milliards de dollars américains en actifs virtuels auprès de la plateforme d'échange de cryptomonnaies Binance, aux alentours du 29 octobre 2026 », a écrit le FBI dans un communiqué.

Le FBI affirme avoir identifié, derrière ce vol sans précédent, le groupe de pirates informatiques nord-coréens connu sous le nom de TraderTraitor. Le FBI a rapporté que les voleurs s'employaient à blanchir les actifs siphonnés, notamment en les convertissant en Ether, la cryptomonnaie du réseau Ethereum. La police américaine a publié une liste d'environ 500 adresses Ethereum « que les acteurs de TraderTraitor sont en train d'utiliser pour blanchir ces actifs volés », et demandé aux acteurs des cryptomonnaies de bloquer les transactions liées à ces adresses.
Donald Trump émet des doutes

Le montant dérobé représente quatre fois celui que TraderTraitor avait aspiré, d'après le FBI, sur la plateforme ByBit en février 2025, soit 1,5 milliard de dollars, à l'époque le vol le plus important en cryptomonnaies.

Le président américain Donald Trump, qui se vante régulièrement d'entretenir de bonnes relations personnelles avec le dirigeant nord-coréen Kim Jong-un, a émis des doutes quant à l'implication de Pyongyang. « Je ne suis pas inquiet. Nous sommes en train d'en apprendre davantage. Nous ne savons pas si c'est la Corée du Nord », a-t-il déclaré à des journalistes depuis sa résidence en Floride tard samedi soir.
L'affaire révèle la vulnérabilité de la plateforme

Après le piratage record de 6,3 milliards de dollars, Binance avait suspendu les retraits pour stopper l'hémorragie. Toutefois, Binance a réautorisé dimanche 1ᵉʳ novembre ses clients à retirer des fonds.

L'affaire a aussi révélé la vulnérabilité de la plateforme, et la reprise partielle des retraits avait des airs de test de la confiance des détenteurs de cryptomonnaies dans le numéro un mondial du secteur. Binance a promis que ses clients ne seraient pas lésés et a racheté des cryptomonnaies pour couvrir les pertes.

Numéro un mondial en volume d'échanges de devises numériques, Binance revendique 335 millions d'utilisateurs. À titre de comparaison, le site Crypto.com évalue à 741 millions le nombre de propriétaires de cryptomonnaies dans le monde. L'attaque contre Binance intervient alors que de nombreux observateurs expriment leurs inquiétudes quant au fait que les capacités toujours plus étendues des modèles d'intelligence artificielle pourraient compromettre les protocoles de sécurité informatique.

items.titel: US midterms 2026: What polls reveal about Democratic, Republican voters
items.anriss: From the economy and cost of living to immigration, polls suggest where American voters agree and disagree.

absaetze.t: Americans will vote in the US midterm elections on Tuesday, with the economy, the cost of living, and immigration among the top issues. While Democrats and Republicans share concerns about the rising cost of living, recent surveys suggest differences in how they view the economy, President Donald Trump, and other key issues.

In an NBC poll released on Sunday, 75 percent of respondents said they were dissatisfied with the state of the US economy, and 51 percent said they were dissatisfied with their personal financial situation.
Other surveys conducted in October also offer a look into how voters from both parties felt about their finances and which issues mattered most.
Here is what we know:
What issues matter most to Democrats and Republicans?
The economy is the main concern for US voters, but Democrats and Republicans vary on the importance of issues like healthcare, immigration, and crime.

A Pew Research Centre survey, conducted between September 28 and October 4, suggested that 84 percent of registered voters considered the economy very important to their midterm vote. It was the top issue for 82 percent of respondents who prefer Republican candidates, and 88 percent for those who back Democrats.
However, the two groups differed on other issues.

About 85 percent of Democratic Party supporters considered the future of democracy very important, compared with 69 percent of Republicans. Healthcare was a priority for 82 percent of Democrats, compared with 53 percent of Republicans.
Republican supporters were more concerned about immigration, with 72 percent saying it was very important, compared with 53 percent of Democrats.
Violent crime was also more important to Republican supporters, at 64 percent, compared with 37 percent Democrats.

A KFF survey, conducted by the Kaiser Family Foundation, an independent nonprofit, from September 16 to 21, suggested 42 percent of registered voter respondents trusted Democrats more to handle healthcare costs, compared with 22 percent who trusted Republicans.
On the cost of living, 39 percent trusted Democrats more, while 25 percent preferred Republicans.
What grade do Democrats and Republicans give Trump’s second term?
Views of President Trump and his economic policies remain divided along party lines.
In the Pew Research Centre survey, 91 percent of Democratic respondents and those who leaned Democratic believed Trump’s economic policies had made things worse.
Among Republican supporters, 39 percent said his policies had improved the economy, 35 percent said they made conditions worse, and 25 percent said they had little effect.
In the November 1 NBC News poll, 40 percent of registered-voter respondents approved of Trump’s overall job performance, compared with 60 percent who disapproved.
How do Democrats and Republicans feel about the economy?
Americans are concerned about rising costs, but Democrats are more likely than Republicans to express negative feelings about economic conditions.
In an October Pew Research survey, 36 percent of Republicans rated the US economy as excellent or good, compared with just 9 percent of Democrats or Democrat-leaning voters.
However, the majority in both groups expressed concern about the cost of essential goods and services.
According to PEW, 82 percent of Democrats and Democratic leaners were concerned about food and consumer prices, compared with 62 percent of Republicans and Republican leaners.
Healthcare costs concerned 80 percent of Democrats and 57 percent of Republicans, while petrol and energy prices worried 81 percent of Democrats and 65 percent of Republicans.

A Fox News poll released on October 14 also had 74 percent of registered voter respondents rating the economy negatively, and 60 percent identified the cost of living as their biggest economic concern.
The November 1 NBC News poll found that 53 percent of Republican respondents were dissatisfied with the state of the economy.

The Pew Research Center also found that abortion and gun policy were less central to Democratic respondents in comparison with 2022. Among Republican voters, education policy and energy policy were less important than they were four years ago.
Are Americans satisfied with their financial situation?
In the NBC poll, 51 percent of registered voters were dissatisfied with their personal financial situation, compared with 49 percent who were satisfied.
It was the first time in 30 years of NBC polling that dissatisfaction with personal finances outweighed satisfaction.

In an NPR/PBS News/Marist poll on October 19-20, 38 percent of likely voters said their finances had gotten worse over the past year, 44 percent said they had remained about the same, and 15 percent said they had improved.
A total of 51 percent of Democratic likely voters said their finances had deteriorated, compared with 21 percent of Republicans.
In a Reuters/Ipsos survey conducted from September 30 to October 5, 71 percent of Democrats and 57 percent of Republicans said their incomes had not kept pace with rising prices.

Eric Ham, a former Democratic congressional staffer and Senate national security adviser, said that Trump’s global tariffs and the US-Israel war on Iran had added to the financial pressure on American households.
“Americans are paying more not just in terms of self-inflicted wounds that President Donald Trump implemented through tariffs, but also if you look at this war of choice,” Ham told Al Jazeera.
Are Democrats or Republicans more enthusiastic about voting?
Democratic voters reported higher enthusiasm about participating in the elections.
In the Marist poll, 91 percent of likely Democratic voters were enthusiastic or very enthusiastic, compared with 86 percent of Republicans and 76 percent of Independents.
John Fury, a former Republican congressional staffer, said the final days of campaigning were focused on turnout.
“This is not a persuasion election. This is a get-out-the base election,” Fury said.

In a KFF survey, Democratic candidate supporters were 25 percentage points more likely than Republican supporters to describe themselves as “more motivated” than usual to vote (63 percent versus 38 percent).
The November 1 NBC News poll also reported high interest in the elections, with 70 percent of registered voters rating their interest at nine or 10 on a 10-point scale.
Who are Americans planning to vote for?
Surveys conducted in the final weeks before the election suggested voters preferred Democratic candidates or Democratic control of Congress over Republicans.

An NBC poll conducted on October 28-30 and published on November 1 suggested that 52 percent of registered voters preferred Democratic control of Congress compared with 45 percent who preferred Republican control.

Similarly, the Reuters/Ipsos poll conducted from October 22 to October 26 suggested that 53 percent of likely voters would vote for or lean towards the Democratic candidates in their district, compared with 44 percent who supported Republicans.
These surveys measure voting sentiment, but they do not reflect the results of the individual races.

absaetze.t: La bande de Gaza est confrontée à une pénurie de billets de banque et à une vraie crise de liquidités. Ces trois dernières années, la guerre menée par Israël a mis à genoux le système bancaire. Les banques ont été fermées. En raison du blocus financier imposé par les Israéliens, les shekels ne rentrent pas. Cela affecte encore un peu plus des conditions de vie déjà très difficiles.
1 min Temps de lecture
Reportage dans la bande de Gaza, Férial Abdu, avec notre correspondante à Jérusalem, Frédérique Misslin

Beaucoup de supermarchés à Gaza n’acceptent plus les billets de banque abîmés. Compliqué pour les mères de famille comme Nour. « Quand je vais au marché, ils refusent de prendre de l'argent si le billet est déchiré ou légèrement abîmé », explique-t-elle.

Avec la guerre, impossible de faire un simple retrait au distributeur. Alors les paiements électroniques se développent. « Aujourd'hui, cela concerne plus de 95 % des opérations bancaires », souligne Mohammed Abu Jayyab, économiste. « Elles sont réalisées via des applications bancaires en ligne. Mais de nombreuses familles n'y ont pas accès pour leurs besoins quotidiens », alerte-t-il.
Commissions exorbitantes

Alaa al-Rafati gère un commerce. Même si les coupures de réseau internet sont très fréquentes, sa clientèle paie en utilisant des applications de transfert d’argent. « Je dirais entre 65 et 70 % », estime le commerçant. « Mais certaines personnes restent complètement en dehors du système car elles n’ont pas de portefeuille électronique, pas de compte bancaire, parfois même pas de téléphone portable. »
Via les canaux informels, les intermédiaires imposent des commissions exorbitantes, plus de 20 % pour convertir des salaires ou des fonds électroniques en espèces.

items.titel: Counter-Drone Laser Weapon Now Guarding Trump’s Mar-a-Lago Alongside SAMs
items.anriss: At least one AeroVironment LOCUST laser counter-drone system is part of the array of anti-air defenses that have popped up around President Donald Trump’s Mar-a-Lago estate in Palm Beach, Florida, in recent weeks. Versions of LOCUST have …

absaetze.t: At least one AeroVironment LOCUST laser counter-drone system is part of the array of anti-air defenses that have popped up around President Donald Trump’s Mar-a-Lago estate in Palm Beach, Florida, in recent weeks. Versions of LOCUST have been seeing steadily increasing use within the U.S. military in recent years, including deployments now along the border with Mexico. Though there has been much progress in the development of practical laser directed-energy weapons in recent years, the technology has continued to face hurdles to more widespread adoption.

The LOCUST system at Mar-a-Lago, which is mounted on a 4×4 Joint Light Tactical Vehicle (JLTV), is seen in two pictures that Getty’s Andrew Harnik took on October 31. When exactly the laser-directed energy weapon was deployed is unclear. Laser Wars was the first to spot the system in one of Harnik’s pictures and confirm its deployment.

Harnik’s main focus was a pair of Humvee-based AN/TWQ-1 Avenger short-range air defense systems on a floating platform in Lake Worth Lagoon near the edge of the estate, which were first deployed there just over two weeks ago. Additional Avengers have also been positioned around Donald J. Trump International Airport, which is situated some three miles to the west. The U.S. military has also set up elements of Counter-Unmanned Aircraft System Fly-Away Kits, including Ku-band radar, electronic support measures (ESM), jammers, and 360-degree infrared search and track systems nearby. TWZ covered the presence of the Avengers and the Fly-Away Kits in a report last Friday.

This heightened security comes amid signs that a new round of major hostilities with Iran could be on the horizon, as well as the run-up to tomorrow’s mid-term elections. The regime in Tehran has threatened Trump’s life on several occasions over the years. The President has already been the subject of several domestic assassination attempts and threats.

“At the request of the U.S. Secret Service (USSS) and under NORAD [the U.S.-Canadian North American Aerospace Defense Command] and USNORTHCOM [U.S. Northern Command] authorities, NORAD and USNORTHCOM recently deployed ground-based air defense [GBAD] assets and Counter-Unmanned Aircraft System capabilities in and around Mar-a-Lago, Florida,” the commands told us in a statement last week. “These assets add a complementary layer of technology to enhance protection. Due to operational security, we are unable to provide additional details. For further detail, we refer you to the USSS.”

“The U.S. Secret Service is operating in a heightened threat environment, and we continuously adapt our protective operations to incorporate cutting-edge tools, technology, and methods to safeguard our protectees,” the Secret Service also told us in a prior statement. “At the request of the U.S. Secret Service, NORAD and U.S. Northern Command are providing Counter-Unmanned Aircraft System capabilities in support of our protective operations.”

The U.S. Army began receiving the JLTV-based versions of LOCUST, along with examples mounted on the smaller 4×4 Infantry Squad Vehicle (ISV) last year through a program called the Army Multi-Purpose High Energy Laser (AMP-HEL). This followed the delivery of palletized LOCUST systems under a rapid prototyping effort called the Palletized-High Energy Laser (P-HEL) in the early 2020s. The Army is now acquiring LOCUST X3 systems under its Enduring-High Energy Laser (E-HEL) program. LOCUST has become something of a star more broadly within the directed energy space across the U.S. military. The U.S. Marine Corps and the U.S. Navy have also been exploring the use of versions of LOCUST in ground-based and shipboard contexts.

To date, all versions of LOCUST consist of a turret with the laser beam projector, as well as built-in electro-optical and infrared video cameras for target acquisition and tracking. The complete system also includes power generation and cooling components. LOCUST variants can also be cued using offboard sensors, including small-form-factor high-frequency radars and passive radio frequency signal detection systems on host vehicles or located off-platform nearby, like what the Fly-Away Kit provides.

The stated power rating for LOCUST varies from version to version, with the latest X3 being a 30-kilowatt type. Though the system is categorized as a high-energy laser, this is at the lower end of the power spectrum for weapons of this type, and it is explicitly geared toward the countering small drones mission set. Layering LOCUST in with other hard- and soft-kill counter-drone and air defense systems in a potentially high-threat area, as we are seeing now at Mar-a-Lago, makes good sense.

As mentioned, Mar-a-Lago is not the first time a LOCUST has been deployed in a real-world context. In 2022, the Army confirmed the operational deployment of two P-HEL systems to unspecified foreign locales. Earlier this year, JLTV- and ISV-based AMP-HELs have appeared along the border with Mexico. One of the systems was part of the chain of events that led to the shutdown of airspace around El Paso, Texas, in February. That incident, in turn, prompted the Pentagon to craft a new agreement with the Federal Aviation Administration (FAA) regarding the use of laser directed energy weapons within the United States.
As TWZ has written in the past:

“In general, laser directed energy weapons offer the promise of functionally unlimited magazine depth, as long as there is sufficient power and cooling capacity. They also present a drastically lower cost-per-intercept proposition compared to traditional anti-air interceptors. This is all advantageous for engaging drones, particularly smaller and cheaper designs that can still present very significant threats. The dangers posed by uncrewed aerial systems are only set to grow as networked swarming and automated targeting capabilities, enabled by advances in artificial intelligence and machine learning, become more accessible. Defenders already face real risks of just being overwhelmed by attacks involving volumes of drones.”

“At the same time, a laser like LOCUST can only engage a single target at once. Lower-powered lasers need to dwell on their targets for a longer period of time in order to cause significant damage by burning a hole in them, as well. This limits the number of targets a single system can engage in a given window of time.”

“In addition, the power of any laser beam drops as it propagates through the atmosphere further and further away from its source. Weather and other environmental factors like smoke and dust can also distort the beam and reduce its power. All of this only adds to the aforementioned dwell time. Adaptive optics, and just more power overall, can help produce useful effects at greater distances, but laser weapons continue to have short ranges, typically measured in handfuls of miles, as a general rule.”

“The Army, as well as other branches of the U.S. military, have repeatedly acknowledged challenges in fielding laser directed energy weapon systems. Sensitivity to vibration, humidity, dust, and sand, as well as fragile optics and cooling demands, have all created further complications for operating and sustaining these systems in real-world environments. “

Army officials just recently touted the benefits of laser directed energy weapons like LOCUST, while also acknowledging again that there is still work to be done at the Association of the U.S. Army’s (AUSA) main annual convention last month.

“Lasers are real. We can do it. We can go out. We can shoot things,” Kirk Williams, Chief Engineer at the Army’s Directed Energy Project Office, another one of the panelists, said. “But what we got to do now is make these systems reliable enough so that the soldiers have the faith in them when they need them, and that’s really the main point that we’re trying to go after right now.”

“We’re getting to the point where the systems are reliable enough, but we still have to make them maintainable and repairable because this is an Army system,” he continued. “It’s going to be on a battlefield. Things are going to break. We can break things in very creative ways, right? So if it’s not reliable, or if it’s not maintainable, if it’s not repairable, that’s a problem.”
At least one LOCUST system is now participating in a very high-profile mission to help protect President Trump.
Contact the author: joe@twz.com

items.titel: Industry needs more consistent demand signal to scale UGV production: Autonomy consortium exec
items.anriss: “I think [industry has] the challenge of understanding what the demand signal is, and then again where to put their dollars,” Warren Sponsler, the COO of NAMC, said in an interview.

absaetze.t: WASHINGTON — The Army’s goal of scaling unmanned ground vehicles is being sabotaged by the service’s inability to provide clear, coherent demand signal to industry, according to an executive at the National Advanced Mobility Consortium (NAMC), a nonprofit organization bridging the Pentagon and industry for ground drone projects.

“I think [industry has] the challenge of understanding what the demand signal is, and then again where to put their dollars. We do talk a lot about these capabilities that the Army has asked for, but they [industry] want to know what’s next,” Warren Sponsler, NAMC’s COO, said in a recent interview.
“[Industry is] trying to align themselves to what’s next. I think that’s probably one of the biggest challenges — just being able to produce at scale.”

Oftentimes companies order parts and put stress on their supply chains before the Army has settled on a contract mechanism or specific capability, Sponsler said. The commitment from industry is there, but the commitment from the Army, or any service for that matter, is not distinct, Sponsler said, which can be rather discouraging for companies.
“Following through on those programs, I think it is critical to maintain that relationship between government and industry,” Sponsler said.

Exercises also sometimes send a murky demand signal, Sponsler said. While the Army has invited industry to demonstrate ground autonomy platforms at several events, the sheer amount of opportunities and unclear mission objectives leave companies unsure where to invest their time and money.

“I think it’s kind of the opposite challenge in many cases,” Sponsler said when asked if he thinks there are enough Army exercises for industry to demo their platforms. “There are so many opportunities right now, and then companies, especially those small companies, are having to make often hard decisions as to which experiments they participate in, and which ones they choose not to.”
He added that “focusing some of the demonstration experimentation activities would be a help” to provide a clear demand signal.

“There’s a lot of opportunities right now that the Army talks about for robotics and autonomy companies to get their stuff out in the field, get user feedback, and I think what [industry] is looking for is, ‘What is that path to scaling? Like, where is that path to revenue?’
“The more that they can describe what capabilities they’re actually looking to field and put together, the better,” he said.
Programs Of Record

Sponsler said the Army’s venture capital acquisition hub, FUZE, has provided a strong example through its xTech competitions for how the service should focus its demonstrations on certain capabilities. For example, xTech has held demonstrations, which are a part of larger competitions that will result in contract awards, for autonomous logistics and sustainment projects and for autonomous breaching. The path to revenue is clear in such cases as companies know they could be the winner of an eventual contract.

Sponsler said he urges companies, especially the nontraditionals, to enter such competitions, but he also urges them pay close attention to the Army’s programs of record for ground autonomy as they are the most indicative of how the Army plans to spend its money. The challenge there: the Army’s programs of record for ground autonomy have also fallen prey to the same lack of clarity as its outreach to industry.

For example, within roughly 18 months, the Army altered its UxS program of record and transformed the former Robotic Combat Vehicle program into the Unmanned Ground Commercial Robotic Vehicle program but then dispersed that program into Project Sustainment and the Engineer Autonomous Breaching Capability program.

The service also relocated its acquisition office for autonomy then stood up a separate Portfolio Acquisition Executive for autonomy and redesignated its Futures and Concepts Command as the new Army Futures and Autonomous Systems Command (FASCOM), which will work in coordination with the Pentagon’s newly established Autonomous Warfare Command (AUTOWARCOM).

The good news, Sponsler said, is that he believes the new AUTOWARCOM, which has yet to be formally established since it requires Congressional approval, and FASCOM will allow the Army and the Pentagon’s autonomy efforts to be better streamlined.
He said the new organizations will help in “providing additional focus to robotics and autonomy integration at the formation level, looking beyond a product and more to a capability,” Sponsler said.

“[It] should also help to align resources and leadership to best prioritize based on the services’ needs. As the Army operates in multiple domains — ground, air, sea — having a [DoD]-level organization with a vision across services should help to mitigate duplicative efforts and better align resources,” he added.

items.titel: 10 Art Books to Curl Up With This November
items.anriss: The publishing industry is already preparing for spring, but we're still stuck on all the delights and challenges of this fall's slate of art books. Editor-in-Chief Hakim Bishara recommends an exploration of Marxist revolutionary Rosa …

absaetze.t: Celia Paul’s latest essay collection from Venice, Salman Toor’s painted worlds, the secret herbarium of Rosa Luxemburg, a new Roy Lichtenstein catalog for old fans, and more.
November 2, 2026 — 6 min read

The publishing industry is already preparing for spring, but we're still stuck on all the delights and challenges of this fall's slate of art books. Editor-in-Chief Hakim Bishara recommends an exploration of Marxist revolutionary Rosa Luxemburg's secret garden of pressed plants, an art form in its own right; critic Natalie Weis sinks into painter Celia Paul's kinetic prose. Catalogs on Salman Toor, Roy Lichtenstein, and more to discover below. —Lakshmi Rivera Amin, associate editor
Roy Lichtenstein: Like New, edited by Alex Da Corte and Meg Onli | Whitney Museum of American Art, November 3

In this publication, the Whitney frames its Roy Lichtenstein show as a “radical” picture as “never before,” made up of a “novel” selection that is “genuinely new” to an audience “newer than ever” (emphasis the museum’s). But the catalog, inspired by the composition notebooks the artist kept to gather inspirational clippings, doesn’t feel academic or overstuffed, and includes beautiful plates — in other words, it’s easy, clean, and classic, all the reasons we’ve always loved Lichtenstein. —Lisa Yin Zhang
Objects of Desire: An Artist in Venice by Celia Paul | New York Review Books, November 17

Celia Paul writes much like she paints, excavating shimmering insights from familiar subjects, in prose that is as haunting and luminous as her portraits. In this memoir, she uses a Venetian residency to examine her relationship with her deceased husband, mother, and first lover (the unnamed Lucian Freud). Grief, guilt, death, and desire stalk the artist through the city’s narrow corridors; once more, Paul seeks self-knowledge through art, literature, and the act of painting. —Natalie Weis
Visualizing Latinx: Creative Practices in Fashion, Film, and Beyond by Arlene Dávila | Duke University Press, October 13

Arlene Dávila begins where most mainstream criticism of Latinx art ends: by challenging the term itself. The professor and curator’s ninth book continues her decades-long critiques of perfunctory “Latinx representation” through shrewd essays on indie filmmakers, fashion designers, and artists — such as Edra Soto and Ela Troyano — who refuse the tropes imposed on their work and often operate outside of the Los Angeles and New York bubbles. Her insights are a reminder to question the narratives that “make Latinx culture palatable for mainstream culture,” to always dig deeper. —Lakshmi Rivera Amin

items.titel: Russia’s security service detains teen over alleged terror plot targeting Moscow museum
items.anriss: The US embassy in Moscow warned of a “credible threat of a mass casualty event” involving the popular Tsaritsyno Museum and Nature Reserve

absaetze.t: Russia’s FSB security service has detained a teenager on charges of threatening Moscow’s Tsaritsyno Museum and Nature Reserve via TikTok after an unusual warning from US officials of a “credible threat of a mass casualty event” on 31 October. The alert was posted on the website of the US embassy in Moscow and social media. Der Spiegel reported that German citizens in Russia had received a similar warning.

On 1 November, the FSB distributed a video, published on sites such as Tass, the official state news agency, showing an unidentified young man being detained, footage of a knife, camouflage and neo-Nazi content on his phone, and his confession to posting “propaganda of Nazism” on his TikTok page. Russia’s National Antiterrorism Committee posted the same footage to its YouTube channel.

The US issued a similar alert several days before an attack that killed at least 149 people in March 2024 during a concert at Crocus City Hall in Moscow. Islamic State claimed responsibility for the attack; before it occurred, Russian President Vladimir Putin denounced the warnings as “outright blackmail”.

In a change reflecting US President Donald Trump’s cooperation with Russia, the FSB in a statement on 1 November, posted on the agency’s website, credited “US law enforcement agencies” for warning of an impending attack at Tsaritsyno: “We are grateful to the American side for the information provided.”

The FSB statement added that “in the interest of public safety, planned cultural events at the museum-reserve have been cancelled, and security measures in the surrounding area have been stepped up”. The museum is typically closed on Mondays, while the surrounding park, known for its rolling hills, fountains and wooded paths, is open daily. Russian media reported that the park reopened on Sunday.

The FSB’s statement claims the detained minor had posted images on TikTok “showing himself wearing tactical gear—including a balaclava, cap, eyewear and headset—while holding an object resembling an automatic weapon” as well as “photographs taken at the Tsaritsyno Museum-Reserve, accompanied by the caption: ‘I found a place’”.

The complex, which was originally intended as a summer residence for Catherine the Great in the 18th century, is consistently ranked as one of Moscow’s most visited tourist sites. Tsaritsyno’s website states that over 7 million people visit the museum and park in southern Moscow annually. The Grand Palace, its centrepiece, is known for its neo-Gothic design by the architect Matvey Kazakov, which remained unfinished after Catherine’s death. Many other buildings on the grounds were designed by Kazakov’s teacher, Vasily Bazhenov, Catherine’s court architect, who was initially commissioned to design the palace before falling out with the Empress.

Some preservationists denounced the glitzy completion of the palace, inaugurated in 2007 with Putin present. It was carried out under Moscow’s mayor at the time, Yury Luzhkov, who was known for monumental construction projects. Although some attempts have been made to show contemporary art at Tsaritsyno, its exhibitions are primarily focused on the tsars and historic Russian folk crafts.

items.titel: Objects reinstalled at Museo Nacional de Colombia following removal by right-wing government
items.anriss: A Bogotá judge ordered that the 63 objects, many related to LGBTQ+ rights and feminism, be put back in their places in the museum’s permanent galleries

absaetze.t: Bogotá’s Museo Nacional de Colombia has reinstalled the 63 objects previously taken down from its permanent galleries over claims of “political indoctrination”. The move followed a court order that reversed the national government's removal of the items on 15 October.

On the evening of 28 October, César Enrique Osorio Ortiz—a judge at Bogotá’s 24th Family Court—ordered Colombia’s cultural ministry and the museum to return the works to their original locations within 48 hours. The ministry complied with the order on Friday (30 October).

The decision came in response to a constitutional-rights case filed by cultural groups and political opponents who had accused the government of the country's far-right President Abelardo de la Espriella of censorship. The judge also ordered both institutions not to remove works based on their content or the views they express.

Among the removed pieces were a pride flag belonging to the activist Elizabeth Castillo, a pen made from a bullet that was used to sign the 2016 peace agreement between the state and the Revolutionary Armed Forces of Colombia, and a poster for the International Day for the Elimination of Violence Against Women.
The removals came amid calls by De la Espriella for a “cultural war” and a “direct blow to ‘wokeism’ and the ideologisation of culture”, an offensive that affected the country’s main museum.

The government’s decision sparked a series of protests during which hundreds of people gathered outside the museum, as well as a joint statement by six museums expressing “deep concern” and calling for the protection of their professional autonomy. The signatories included the Modern art museums of Bogotá, Barranquilla, Cartagena, Medellín and Tolima, as well as the Museo Rayo.

Marielsa Castro Vizcarra, the chief curator of the Museo de Arte Moderno de Medellín (which signed the joint statement), tells The Art Newspaper that the cultural sector responded quickly, from street protests to the statement and the involvement of the International Committee for Museums and Collections of Modern Art. Castro described the incident as “a precedent we need to take into account” and “an authoritarian way of spreading fear”.

According to the judge's ruling, the artefacts had been removed “without a documented curatorial justification” in a decision that “disregarded the constitutional protection of cultural expressions”. The court did not rule out future changes to the exhibitions, provided they are properly justified and not based on the authorities’ objections to the works’ content.
“No government owns our history!” wrote Gabriel Becerra, a left-wing lawmaker behind the constitutional-rights case, in a post on X welcoming the court’s decision.

items.titel: 10 Art Shows to See in Upstate New York This November
items.anriss: As autumn unfolds across the East Coast, people around the United States are visiting the polls. May we strip the monsters of power and steer this nation out of its ghoulish ambiance and toward soulful care, not continued scare. In step …

absaetze.t: Julia Whitney Barnes’s organic paradise, Emily Nomer’s mystical geometric paintings, Maria Molteni’s conversations with the divine, and more
November 2, 2026 — 9 min read

As autumn unfolds across the East Coast, people around the United States are visiting the polls. May we strip the monsters of power and steer this nation out of its ghoulish ambiance and toward soulful care, not continued scare. In step with the changing times, a robust round of exhibitions in Upstate New York invites you to experience the treats of the season. At Ipso Facto Gallery in Hudson, artists explore creative modalities for surviving the technological hellscape of contemporary life, while Public Private Gallery presents outrageous sculptural works by legendary artists Judy Pfaff and Michael David. Ann Street Gallery features dynamic works by the three artists chosen for their 2026 Emerging Artist Fellowship, and Tyte Gallery showcases a series of lush botanical works on paper by Julia Whitney Barnes. Geometrically inspired paintings by Emily Nomer at Gallery 40 yield bright mystical visions, while a group show at Yellow Studio Arts Center celebrates the commonplace as muse. To all those who fear these hellish times, no more tricks! We conjure our determination and perseverance in the face of ghastly evil!
The TV Glow Sees Me
Ipso Facto Gallery, 362 ½ Warren Street, Hudson, New YorkThrough November 22

Remember life before the internet and obsessive screen time? The TV Glow Sees Me presents the work of five artists who consider how to find themselves amid the “technological hellscape of rapid expansion,” as curator Hannah Studnick puts it in the press release. Featuring mixed-media artworks that reflect a digital culture overflowing with miscellaneous mayhem, Jesse Morsberger’s painting “Up Late” (2026) is a faithful embodiment of our current society: A boy sits alone in a dark room facing the eerie glow of an empty screen. In a crimson-hued scene by Mina Watanabe DeVore, “Look Up” (2026), two youthful figures take a selfie in a graffiti-laden bathroom reminiscent of the legendary Manhattan music club CBGB. Other highlights include Jackson Daughety’s “Where is MrBeast When You Need Him” (2023), a gestural abstract work on stitched canvas, and Allyson Packer’s “Subtropolis 02” (2025), a mash-up sculptural work that includes an LED tube behind a sublimation print in which braces-heavy mouths above a car smash into an unknown object in a bizarre vision that defies explanation.
